evidenceAudit.scope: Adults on first-line anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) in India who develop raised liver enzymes or jaundice: diagnosis, when to stop drugs, an interim liver-safe regimen when TB treatment cannot wait, stepwise reintroduction, and ATT choice in chronic liver disease. Built on the ICMR ATT-Related Hepatitis workflow (March 2022), with drug doses from the ICMR National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) drug-sensitive TB workflow and NTEP weight bands for levofloxacin.
findings: Diagnostic thresholds with and without symptoms, risk factors, baseline and viral hepatitis tests, monitoring, stopping hepatotoxic drugs, interim non-hepatotoxic drugs, Child-Pugh-based regimens and scoring, reintroduction criteria, sequence and doses, and do's and don'ts checked against the ICMR ATT Hepatitis STW (March 2022).
Ethambutol and streptomycin mg/kg doses from the ICMR NTEP drug-sensitive TB STW; levofloxacin weight-band doses from the NTEP knowledge base (longer oral M/XDR-TB regimen table).
unverifiedSections: The ICMR STW names fluoroquinolones, ethambutol and aminoglycosides for the interim regimen without doses; levofloxacin doses are taken from the NTEP drug-resistant TB weight-band table.
Cycloserine and capreomycin doses for Child-Pugh C regimens are not given; specialist only.
The source drops some inequality symbols; thresholds are read as 'at or above'.
Drug cautions and contraindications without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.
US labels (DailyMed) were used where Indian sources give no dose; confirm against the Indian product label (CDSCO) and hospital formulary.

pathophysiology.summary: Isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide can all injure the liver. ATT-induced hepatitis is diagnosed when transaminases rise to 3 times the upper limit with symptoms (or bilirubin 2 times the upper limit with jaundice), or to 5 times without symptoms (ICMR STW). Hepatotoxic drugs are stopped; if TB is severe and treatment cannot pause, a liver-safe interim regimen of ethambutol, a fluoroquinolone and an aminoglycoside is used. When enzymes settle, drugs are reintroduced one at a time — rifampicin, then isoniazid, then pyrazinamide — to find the culprit. Viral hepatitis must be excluded.
keyMechanisms: Isoniazid metabolites (via acetylation) cause direct hepatocyte injury.
Rifampicin can cause cholestasis and enhances isoniazid toxicity by enzyme induction.
Alcohol, malnutrition, HIV, older age and existing liver disease reduce liver reserve.

symptoms: Abdominal pain, vomiting, unexplained fatigue (ICMR STW)
physicalSigns: Signs of chronic liver disease: splenomegaly, ascites, oedema (risk factors)
redFlags: Jaundice with coagulopathy or encephalopathy: refer immediately (ICMR STW)
Severe hepatitis: do not reintroduce pyrazinamide (ICMR STW)
precipitants: HIV, injecting drug use, older age (ICMR STW)

differentials.condition: Acute viral hepatitis A or E
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Immunoglobulin M (IgM) anti-HAV or IgM anti-HEV positive (ICMR STW).
Heavy drinking; aspartate aminotransferase (AST) greater than alanine aminotransferase (ALT).
Other hepatotoxic medicines (for example co-trimoxazole, antiretrovirals).

differentials.condition: TB of the liver or biliary obstruction

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: AST or ALT 3 times baseline or upper limit of normal (ULN), or jaundice with bilirubin 2 times ULN.
AST or ALT 5 times baseline or ULN.
AST and ALT below 2 times ULN and bilirubin normal.

Child A (score 1–6): 9 months HRE, or 2 months HRE then 7 months HR. Child B (7–10): one hepatotoxic drug — 2 months isoniazid or rifampicin with ethambutol and an aminoglycoside, then 10 months isoniazid or rifampicin with ethambutol. Child C (11–15): no hepatotoxic drugs — 18–24 months ethambutol, fluoroquinolone, cycloserine and an aminoglycoside or capreomycin.
Bilirubin under 2 / 2–3 / over 3 mg/dL; albumin over 3.5 / 2.8–3.5 / under 2.8 g/dL; INR under 1.7 / 1.7–2.2 / over 2.2; ascites none / slight / moderate; encephalopathy none / grade 1–2 / grade 3–4.

ruleIn.normalValue: AST and ALT under 40 U/L; bilirubin 0.3–1.2 mg/dL
ruleIn.expectedFinding: AST or ALT 3 times ULN with symptoms or 5 times without; bilirubin 2 times ULN with jaundice
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines ATT hepatitis; repeat 1 week after stopping and at each reintroduction step (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Stop hepatotoxic drugs
actions: Stop isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide (ICMR STW).
Jaundice with coagulopathy or encephalopathy: refer to a higher centre immediately (ICMR STW).
Exclude viral hepatitis and check INR and ultrasound (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Is TB treatment urgent?
actions: Life- or organ-threatening TB (for example meningitis, miliary): start liver-safe drugs — fluoroquinolone, ethambutol and an aminoglycoside such as streptomycin (ICMR STW).
Not urgent: repeat liver tests after 1 week, then reintroduce (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Reintroduce one drug at a time
clinicalManagement.timeframe: When AST and ALT under 2 times ULN and bilirubin normal
actions: Rifampicin 10 mg/kg; after 1 week, if liver tests normal, add isoniazid 5 mg/kg; after another week, if normal, add pyrazinamide 25 mg/kg (ICMR STW).
Alternative: start each drug at low dose and reach full dose after 3 days (ICMR STW).
After severe hepatitis (liver failure, coagulopathy, altered sensorium), do not reintroduce pyrazinamide (ICMR STW).
Count treatment duration only from the start of full ATT (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Underlying chronic liver disease
actions: Score Child-Pugh and choose the regimen by class (ICMR STW).
Counsel on symptoms; monitor liver tests (ICMR STW).

branches.label: Interim liver-safe regimen
branches.entryCriteria: ATT hepatitis when TB treatment cannot be paused (ICMR STW).

branches.entryCriteria: AST and ALT below 2 times ULN and bilirubin normal (ICMR STW).

branches.label: Reintroduction — step 2 (after 1 week)

medicationPlan.note: Reintroduction doses and sequence are from the ICMR ATT Hepatitis STW; ethambutol and streptomycin doses from the ICMR NTEP STW (maximum doses from its paediatric table); levofloxacin from NTEP weight bands. Once the culprit is found, the regimen is rebuilt without it under specialist and NTEP guidance. Not clinically reviewed.

learningObjectives: Decide when an interim regimen is needed.
keyPoints: 3 times ULN with symptoms, 5 times without.
Reintroduce rifampicin, then isoniazid, then pyrazinamide, a week apart.
pitfalls: Stopping all TB treatment in TB meningitis without an interim regimen.
Missing viral hepatitis A or E.
Counting interrupted weeks toward treatment duration.
